t: Delete Tree Nodes — Subtree Sum Pruning via DFS
o: We must delete every subtree whose total value sum is zero, then count remaining nodes. Note the deletion rule: if a subtree is deleted, all its descendants vanish with it, so a node survives only if its own subtree sum is nonzero. In Example 1, node 1's subtree sums to -2+0 = -2 (nonzero) but node 3 alone sums to 0 and is removed; nodes 4,5,6 have subtree sums -2,-1,-2... actually recomputing: node 2's subtree sums to 4-2-1-1 = 0, so it and children are removed; node 1's subtree sums to -2+0 = -2, kept; root keeps 1 + (-2) = ... final answer counts surviving nodes: root and node 1 → 2. Constraints allow n up to 10^4, so any O(n) or O(n log n) traversal works; recursion depth could reach n = 10^4 which may overflow default stack limits in some languages, so an iterative DFS/BFS bottom-up pass is safer.
k: A node survives iff its entire subtree sum is nonzero; deletion cascades to all descendants automatically.
Compute each subtree's (sum, count) bottom-up in one post-order pass over the tree.
Process nodes in reverse topological order (children before parents) to avoid recursion depth issues.

a.i: Do a standard DFS from the root returning (subtreeSum, keptCount). For each node, combine children results; if the total sum is zero return count 0 for this whole subtree, otherwise return the accumulated count plus 1. This directly encodes the rule that deleting a subtree removes all descendants.
s: Build an adjacency list of children from parent[].
DFS(node) returns [sum, count] of the subtree rooted at node.
Initialize sum = value[node], count = 1; add each child's returned sum and count.
If sum == 0, return [0, 0]; else return [sum, count].
Answer is the count returned at the root.
a.t: O(n) — each node is visited exactly once during the DFS.
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency list plus O(h) recursion stack, worst case O(n) for a path-shaped tree.

a.i: Since parent[i] < i is not guaranteed in general trees, we can't just iterate backwards; instead compute node depth/processing order via BFS, then process nodes deepest-first so every child is finalized before its parent. This avoids recursion entirely, making it robust against deep trees.
s: Build children adjacency list and run BFS from root to get a processing order where parents precede children.
Initialize sum[i] = value[i] and cnt[i] = 1 for all nodes.
Iterate the BFS order in reverse (children before parents).
For each node u, add sum[u] and cnt[u] into its parent's accumulators.

After processing, for each node with sum == 0 set cnt to 0 and propagate: since we process bottom-up, when a child's cnt becomes 0 its contribution was already added — instead check at parent time: skip adding children whose cnt is 0. Answer is cnt[0].
a.t: O(n) — BFS ordering plus one reverse pass, each node handled once.
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency list, order array, sum/count arrays; no recursion stack.

w: In an interview, start with the recursive DFS (simplest to reason about), then mention the iterative version if asked about deep trees or stack limits. Key pitfalls: (1) forgetting that a zero-sum subtree's removal also zeroes out contributions to ancestors — handle by discarding both sum and count together; (2) using 32-bit ints for sums — up to 10^4 nodes × 10^5 magnitude can exceed int range in C++/Java, use long; (3) assuming parent[i] < i — not guaranteed by the problem, so don't rely on reverse index iteration without a BFS order. Edge cases: single node with value 0 returns 0; all-zero tree returns 0. Follow-ups might ask for a solution with O(1) extra space beyond output, or handling forests / multiple roots.
